message.content:
Lions (Panthera leo) belong to the order **Carnivora** (family Felidae), while zebras (Equus quagga) belong to the order **Perissodactyla** (family Equidae).  
Their most recent common ancestor is therefore a member of the larger clade that contains both of those orders – the Laurasiatheria – and dates back to the early Eocene, roughly **55–60 million years ago**.

That ancestor would have been a small, probably insect‑eating mammal that lived on the ancient supercontinent Laurasia. It was not yet specialized as a big cat or a grazing horse; it simply possessed the basic mammalian body plan that later diversified into the distinct lineages that produced modern carnivorans (including lions) and perissodactyls (including zebras).
message.reasoning:
The user asks: "What is the common ancestor of lion and zebra?" They want an answer. We can provide a general evolutionary biology answer: The common ancestor of lions (Panthera leo) and zebras (Equus quagga) would be a common ancestor within the order Carnivora for lions and the order Perissodactyla for zebras? Wait, lions are mammals, specifically within the family Felidae, subfamily Pantherinae. Zebras are equids, family Equidae, order Perissodactyla. So their common ancestor would be at the level of the class Mammalia, but more precisely the last common ancestor of the two species would be a mammal from the group that gave rise to both carnivores and perissodactyls. That would be a common ancestor of the clade that includes both Carnivora and Perissodactyla. That clade is called the Laurasiatheria? Actually, Carnivora and Perissodactyla are part of the superorder Laurasiatheria. Within Laurasiatheria, the last common ancestor of Carnivora and Perissodactyla would be a member of the group that gave rise to the clade that includes the orders Carnivora and Perissodactyla. That might be the last common ancestor of the clade that includes the orders Carnivora, Perissodactyla, and others like Cetartiodactyla. But we can say: The last common ancestor of lions and zebras was a small, probably insectivorous mammal that lived around 60 million years ago, belonging to the group that eventually split into the lineages leading to modern carnivorans and perissodactyls.

We can mention that the last common ancestor of all placental mammals is older (~66 million years). But the last common ancestor of the two specific species is likely a small, early ungulate-like mammal that existed around 55-60 million years ago. We can also mention that the last common ancestor of the families Felidae and Equidae would have been a mammal that existed before the divergence of the two lineages, which occurred during the Eocene epoch.

Thus answer: The common ancestor of lions and zebras is a small, probably insectivorous mammal that lived about 55-60 million years ago, belonging to the clade that gave rise to the Laurasiatherian mammals, including the ancestors of both the Carnivora (lion lineage) and Perissodactyla (zebra lineage).
